title: Health Assessment & Nursing Skills: Neurologic Assessment—Mental Status, Pupils, Strength & Acute Change
html:
A neurologic assessment evaluates arousal, cognition, communication, cranial-nerve function, movement, sensation, coordination, balance, and change over time. The RN begins observing as soon as the client is encountered: posture, facial symmetry, spontaneous movement, speech, attention, behavior, and response to the environment are already neurologic data. The most meaningful finding is often a new change from the client’s reliable baseline.

Learning goals

  • Differentiate level of consciousness from orientation and cognition.
  • Assess speech, pupils, facial symmetry, motor strength, sensation, coordination, and gait safely.
  • Use a focused neurologic screen and recognize when a more structured tool is required.
  • Account for language, sensory ability, medication, metabolic, and developmental factors.
  • Recognize time-sensitive neurologic change and initiate prompt escalation.
  • Document objective findings, timing, interventions, and reassessment.

Stability and time come first

Assess airway, breathing, circulation, and responsiveness before proceeding with a routine examination. A sudden decrease in responsiveness, new seizure activity, new facial droop, unilateral weakness or numbness, new inability to speak or understand, abrupt vision or balance change, a sudden severe headache, or new unequal or nonreactive pupils can signal a neurologic emergency. Stop the routine sequence, maintain safety, obtain immediate assistance, and initiate the appropriate protocol.

Record the last known well time
For a possible acute stroke, identify the exact time the client was last known to be at the neurologic baseline—not merely the time the deficit was discovered. Communicate this time with the observed deficits and activate the emergency pathway without waiting to complete every cranial-nerve test.

Ask a focused neurologic history

Clarify onset, progression, duration, triggers, and prior episodes of headache, dizziness or vertigo, fainting, seizure, weakness, numbness, tingling, tremor, balance change, falls, vision or hearing change, swallowing difficulty, memory change, confusion, and speech or language difficulty. Ask what the client was doing when symptoms began and what function has changed.

Review prior neurologic conditions and baseline deficits, head injury, recent surgery or procedures, infection, diabetes, cardiovascular risks, alcohol or substance exposure, sleep, nutrition, and prescribed or nonprescribed medications. Sedatives, opioids, anticholinergic effects, withdrawal, hypoglycemia, hypoxemia, infection, electrolyte disturbance, and other systemic problems can alter neurologic findings. The RN assesses reversible threats and does not assume every change is caused by a primary brain disorder.

Level of consciousness is not the same as orientation

Level of consciousness describes arousal and the stimulus required to obtain a response. Note whether the client is alert, drowsy but easily aroused, difficult to arouse, or unresponsive, using the organization’s approved terminology. Assess the quality and appropriateness of the response. A client can be awake but confused, or unable to answer orientation questions because of aphasia, hearing loss, language difference, or developmental factors.

Orientation assesses awareness of person, place, time, and situation when appropriate. Ask open questions rather than yes/no questions that can be guessed. Compare with baseline and interpret errors in context. Repeatedly asking orientation questions alone is not a complete neurologic reassessment.

Observe attention, ability to follow commands, short- and longer-term memory as indicated, thought organization, affect, behavior, and speech. Determine whether speech is slurred, words are incorrect, comprehension is impaired, or voice quality has changed. Use the client’s preferred language and a qualified interpreter. Ensure hearing aids, glasses, and communication devices are available before labeling a response abnormal.

Use structured tools correctly

A structured scale such as the Glasgow Coma Scale may be required for head injury or impaired consciousness. Follow the exact tool instructions and report the eye, verbal, and motor components as well as the total when policy requires. The lowest total GCS is 3, not zero. Document factors that limit testing, such as an artificial airway, sedation, paralysis, language barrier, swelling, or preexisting deficit.

A score does not replace airway assessment or the rest of the examination. Trend the same tool under comparable conditions. A change in component response may matter even when the total changes little. Use stroke-specific or delirium tools only when trained and according to policy; do not improvise scoring.

Assess pupils deliberately

Inspect pupil size, shape, and equality before shining light. Test direct and consensual response with an appropriate light source while protecting comfort and vision. Record actual size in millimeters when required and whether each pupil is brisk, sluggish, or nonreactive according to local terminology. Accommodation is assessed only when appropriate to the examination.

Medication, eye surgery, trauma, low ambient light, and a documented baseline difference can affect pupils. New anisocoria, a new sluggish or absent response, or pupil change accompanied by declining consciousness, severe headache, or focal deficit requires urgent action. The acronym PERRLA is useful only if every represented element was actually assessed; specific documentation is safer than copying a normal phrase.

Screen cranial-nerve function through purposeful tasks

A routine screen may include visual fields and eye movement, facial sensation and symmetry, hearing, palate and voice quality, shoulder elevation, and tongue position as indicated. Ask the client to smile, show teeth, raise eyebrows, close eyes, or perform other standardized actions when appropriate, comparing sides. Observe for droop, gaze deviation, abnormal eye movement, dysarthria, voice change, choking, or difficulty managing secretions.

Swallowing safety is a priority. With a new neurologic deficit, keep the client from oral food, fluids, and medications until the approved swallowing screen or evaluation is completed. Do not test swallowing by casually giving water when the client has new facial weakness, wet voice, coughing, drooling, or reduced alertness.

Compare motor function on both sides

Observe spontaneous movement, muscle bulk, tone, tremor, and symmetry. Assess hand grasps and upper- and lower-extremity strength against equal resistance when safe, following a consistent grading scale. Ask about pain or orthopedic limitations before applying resistance. Compare corresponding muscle groups and distinguish inability from pain, poor understanding, fatigue, or effort.

Pronator drift can reveal subtle upper-extremity weakness when appropriate: the client extends both arms with palms upward and eyes closed while the RN observes for downward drift or pronation. Stop if the client becomes unsafe. New unilateral weakness, drift, or loss of movement is more urgent than a chronic stable deficit and should be correlated with facial, speech, sensory, and consciousness findings.

Assess sensation without leading the answer

Ask about numbness, tingling, burning, altered temperature, or changed body awareness. With the client’s eyes closed and understanding confirmed, compare the same light-touch stimulus at corresponding distal and proximal sites. Vary the timing so the client is not responding from rhythm alone. Avoid injured skin and use a safe stimulus.

Map the location and boundaries of altered sensation. Never use sharp objects improvised from the environment. Specialized pain, temperature, vibration, or cortical sensory testing requires the correct equipment and technique. New unilateral sensory loss or numbness with weakness, speech change, or vascular compromise requires prompt escalation.

Check coordination, balance, and gait only when safe

Finger-to-nose, rapid alternating movements, heel-to-shin, and other tasks may assess coordination when clinically indicated. Interpret performance with strength, vision, comprehension, pain, and range of motion. A poor result does not automatically identify the lesion or cause.

Review fall risk before standing the client. Use needed footwear, gait belt, assistive device, and assistance according to policy. Observe rising, stance, balance, step pattern, arm swing, turning, and tolerance. Do not perform Romberg or gait testing on a client who cannot stand safely, has an acute focal deficit, or is unstable; document why the test was deferred.

Recognize acute change as a pattern

High-risk clusters include facial asymmetry plus arm drift and speech change; decreasing arousal plus shallow respirations and pinpoint pupils; fever plus new confusion and hypotension; headache plus vomiting, pupil change, or weakness; or a fall followed by worsening alertness. Check glucose, oxygenation, vital signs, medication exposure, and other rapidly reversible threats under the appropriate protocol while emergency evaluation proceeds. One possible mimic does not justify delaying time-sensitive care.

Maintain airway and aspiration precautions, protect from falls or injury, avoid oral intake when swallowing is uncertain, identify last known baseline, and communicate exact findings and timing. Reassess the same components frequently enough for the acuity and policy. Improvement in orientation does not prove that strength, pupils, airway protection, or speech has normalized.

Respect delegation boundaries

Assistive personnel can report behavior, mobility, or a change from usual function and may collect selected routine measurements within policy. The RN performs and interprets the neurologic assessment, validates changes, chooses the required focused or structured examination, initiates safety measures, escalates concerns, and evaluates outcomes. A report that a client is “sleepier than usual” requires RN follow-up, not simple documentation.

Document findings that can be repeated

Record the time and context; level of consciousness and response to stimulus; orientation and communication method; speech and command following; pupil size and reactivity by side; facial symmetry; strength grade and side; drift; sensation location; coordination and gait; baseline comparison; tool name and components; limiting factors; last known well time; safety actions; notifications; and response.

For example: “0815: New right facial droop, right arm drift, and slurred speech; follows one-step commands. Pupils 3 mm, equal and brisk. Last known at documented baseline 0745. Client kept NPO and in bed; point-of-care glucose obtained per stroke protocol; stroke response activated at 0817. Airway patent; RN remained present.” This preserves observable cues and time without assigning an unconfirmed diagnosis.

Clinical example

An older adult who was conversational at breakfast becomes inattentive and drowsy. The RN does not assume dementia or normal aging. The RN assesses airway, breathing, circulation, arousal, pupils, speech, symmetry, strength, sensation, vital signs, oxygenation, glucose under protocol, medication timing, and recent events; compares with the morning baseline; institutes safety measures; communicates the acute change; and reassesses after interventions.
